extracted.subtask_description: Practical editorial rules for spelling, participles, and punctuation (periods, commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, apostrophes, quotation marks). Intended to guide house style and mechanical correctness in published prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participles retaining final e
rubrics_metrics.description: participles retain the final e in the primary word:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: agreeing, hieing, singeing, dyeing, hoeing, tingeing, eyeing, shoeing, vieing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participles omitting final e
rubrics_metrics.description: The following participles illustrate those that omit the e before the terminal:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: abridging, changing, judging, acknowledging, encouraging, mistaking, aging, glazing, moving, arguing, gluing, organizing, awing, biting, grudging, icing, owing, trudging, bluing, issuing, truing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred spellings (selected forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists many preferred spellings and variant forms (mostly American usage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive example list includes: abridgment; acknowledgment; aerie/Aeolian; aluminum; armor/armour notes; color/colour variants; catalog/catelogue style choices; practice, rumor, traveler, theater, theater/theatre, etc. Use the forms listed in the manual as publisher-preferred spellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make one word of certain compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: NOTE. — Make one word of 'anyone,' 'someone,' 'everyone,' 'today,' 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'cannot' (see 204).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between 'sometimes' and 'some time(s).' Follow the one-word forms indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate terminations -ise and -ize
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between the terminations -ise and -ize as follows:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell with -ise for words like advertise, comprise, enterprise, advise, despise, supervise, surprise, etc. Spell with -ize (-yze) for words like aggrandize, analyze, characterize, familiarize, organize, realize, symbolize, utilize, etc. Follow the provided lists for which words take which ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation printed in same style as preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word, letter, or character immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: quotes and punctuation should match the preceding typeface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period marks end of a complete sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a complete sentence (see 125).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use period to terminate complete sentences; see related rules for exceptions and special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods after abbreviations (general rule and exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations, except in cases where a mechanical necessity compels the omission of a letter or letters in the middle of a word for which there is no recognized abbreviated form; such omission is indicated by an apostrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metric symbols as abbreviations (with period), but not chemical symbols, nor the phrase 'per cent,' nor formats of books (examples provided). Footnote: exceptions for certain journal practices and technical matters are given (e.g., recognized abbreviations for linguistic epochs, MS).

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals, even if having the value of ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after running-heads and certain heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads; after centered headlines; after side-heads set in separate lines; after cut-in heads; after box-heads in tables; and after superscriptions and legends which do not form a complete sentence; after date lines at top of communications, and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See section references for explanation (279-83, 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Period placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The period is placed inside the quotation marks; and inside the parentheses when the matter inclosed is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule stated as 'This is a rule without exception.' Examples provided to clarify usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point use
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point is used to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Long live the king!' 'How funny this seems!' The exclamation point is placed inside quotation marks or parentheses when part of the quoted or parenthetical matter; otherwise outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogation point use
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogation point is used to mark a query, or to express a doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect questions should not be followed by an interrogation point. The interrogation point should be placed inside the quotation marks or parentheses only when it is part of the quotation or parenthetical matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon usage and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon is used to 'mark a discontinuity of grammatical construction greater than that indicated by the semicolon and less than that indicated by the period.' Common uses: (i) to emphasize a close connection between two complete clauses; (2) to separate a clause complete from an illustrative second clause; (3) to introduce a formal statement, extract, speech in dialogue, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a conjunction like 'that' immediately connects clauses, do not use a colon. Use a comma before a quoted clause in the middle of a sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon as substitute for 'namely' or similar words
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon often takes the place of an implied 'namely,' 'as follows,' 'for instance,' or similar phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where such a word or phrase is used, it should be followed by a colon if what follows consists of one or more grammatically complete clauses; otherwise, by a comma (see 145). Examples contrast when to use colon vs comma (viz., etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon after salutatory phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon after the salutatory phrase at the beginning of a letter, and after the introductory remark of a speaker addressing the chairman or the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'MY DEAR MR. BROWN:' and 'Mr. Chairman, Ladies, and Gentlemen:'

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon between chapter:verse and hours:minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a centered colon between chapter and verse in Scripture passages, and between hours and minutes in time indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon between place and publisher in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon between the place of publication and the publisher's name in literary and bibliographical references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan), II, 97.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon placement relative to quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon should be placed outside the quotation marks, unless a part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate exception when colon is within quoted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon use to mark division stronger than comma
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon is used to mark the division of a sentence somewhat more independent than that marked by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show semicolon linking related independent clauses where comma insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in complex enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerations use a semicolon between the different links, if these consist of more than a few words closely connected, especially if individual clauses contain any punctuation mark of less value than a period, or an exclamation or interrogation point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long example of international commission membership demonstrates when semicolons are needed between items containing commas or parenthetical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in Scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scripture references a semicolon is used to separate passages containing chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon placement relative to quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The semicolon should be placed outside the quotation marks or parentheses, unless a part of the quotation or parenthetical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows the same logic as other terminal punctuation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma general function
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is 'used to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, the marking of which contributes to clearness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many illustrative examples show how commas change meaning by bracketing phrases, separating clauses, and indicating pauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate proper nouns referring to different individuals/places
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals or places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'To John, Smith was always kind'; 'To America, Europe awards the prize...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial (Oxford) comma rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'and,' 'or,' and 'nor' connecting the last two links in a sequence of three or more; or all the links in a series of greater length, or where each individual link consists of several words; always put a comma before 'etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Tom, Dick, and Harry'; 'either copper, silver, or gold.' Note: do not use a comma where 'and' serves to connect brief close-knit links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions such as 'and,' 'but,' 'if,' 'while,' 'as,' 'whereas,' 'since,' etc., especially if a change of subject takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and counterexamples show when commas are required or omitted (e.g., when the preceding clause is not logically complete without the conjunction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with introductory adverbs/parenthetical connectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Words/phrases like 'now,' 'then,' 'however,' 'indeed,' 'therefore,' 'moreover,' etc., should be followed by a comma when standing at the beginning of a sentence or clause to introduce an inference or explanation, and should be placed between commas when wedged into the middle of a sentence to mark a distinct break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: do not use a comma when connection is logically close or with certain adverbs used directly after verbs/adjectives. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma before 'rather' in specific constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is preferably omitted before 'rather' in such an expression as 'The time-value is to be measured in this way rather than by the time-equivalent of the strata.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary comma before 'rather' in similar constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between adjectives: coordinate vs cumulative
rubrics_metrics.description: If among several adjectives preceding a noun the last bears a more direct relation to the noun than the others, it should not be preceded by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the admirable political institutions' (no comma), 'a handsome, wealthy young man' (comma between adjectives of equal rank).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to set off participial clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Participial clauses, especially those that contain an explanation of the main clause, should usually be set off by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Being asleep, he did not hear him'; 'Exhausted by a hard day's work, he slept like a stone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'not' introducing an antithetical clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'not' introducing an antithetical clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Men addict themselves to inferior pleasures, not because they deliberately prefer them, but because...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas for parenthetical, adverbial, or appositional phrases (and dash usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: For parenthetical, adverbial, or appositional clauses or phrases use commas to indicate structurally disconnected but logically integral interpolations; use dashes to indicate both structurally and logically disconnected insertions; never use the two together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate comma use vs dash use; do not combine comma and dash around the same insertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate identical or closely similar words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two identical or closely similar words, even if the sense or grammatical construction does not require such separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Whatever is, is good.'; 'What he was, is not known.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma around complementary/qualifying adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: In adjectival phrases, a complementary, qualifying, delimiting, or antithetical adjective added to the main epithet preceding a noun should be preceded and followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This harsh, though perfectly logical, conclusion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between coordinate clauses ending in a governing/modifying word
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more coordinate clauses ending in a word governing or modifying another word in a following clause should be separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '... a shallow body of water connected with, but well protected from, the open sea.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to separate two numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarly, use a comma to separate two numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'In 1905, 347 teachers attended the convention'; 'November 1, 1905.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to indicate omission of words
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is employed to indicate the omission, for brevity or convenience, of a word or words the repetition of which is not essential to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two.' Often smooth enough constructions do not require commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before brief direct quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct quotation, maxim, or similar expression, when brief, should be separated from the preceding part of the sentence by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'God said, Let there be light.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'of' with residence or position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before 'of' in connection with residence or position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mr. and Mrs. McIntyre, of Detroit, Mich.; President Hadley, of Yale University.' Exceptions when place-name is part of name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between consecutive pages in references (do not use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a comma between consecutive pages in literary references, but use the en dash; an exception may be made for scriptural references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'pp. 4, 7-8, 10;' use en dash for ranges 'pp. 113-16.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma after digits indicating thousands
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma after digits indicating thousands, except when used as a date or in a page reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '1,276; 10,419; January, 1909; p. 2461.' Notes mention certain journals' exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma separate month and year
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate month and year, and similar time divisions by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'November, 1905; New Year's Day, 1906.' Note: certain journals do not use a comma between month and year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma in signatures/address lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma in signatures and at the beginning of articles after author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after address followed by a date line, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show format for signature block without commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement with quotation marks and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks, but following the parentheses, if the context requires it at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard American-style placement: commas inside closing quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe for contractions and omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe is used to mark the omission of a letter or letters in the contraction of a word, or of figures in a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ne'er, don't, 'twas; m'f'g; the class of '96.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming the possessive case
rubrics_metrics.description: The possessive case of nouns, common and proper, is formed by the addition of an apostrophe, or apostrophe and s (see 113).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's word; horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe; Themistocles' era; Jones's farms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural of numerals and rare coinages with apostrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: The plural of numerals, and of rare or artificial noun-coinages, is formed by the aid of an apostrophe and s; of proper nouns of more than one syllable ending in a sibilant, by adding an apostrophe alone (monosyllabic proper names ending in a sibilant add es; others, s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the 1900's; in two's and three's; the Y.M.C.A.'s; 'the Tommy Atkins' of England' (but: the Rosses and the Macdougals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash denotes sudden break/transition
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash is used to denote 'a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, or an abrupt change in its construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected or epigrammatic turn of sentiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate dramatic pauses, appositions, or epigrammatic turns. Use dash sparingly and for emphasis or abrupt transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dashes for parenthetical clauses that are logically and structurally independent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes (rarely parentheses) for parenthetical clauses which are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show dashes bracketing strong interruptions; see rule 150 for comparison with commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dash to introduce emphatic or explanatory repeated phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause added to lend emphasis to, or to explain or expand, a word or phrase occurring in the main clause, which word or phrase is then repeated, should be introduced by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '... more important as the sources for history — the history of events and ideas'; '... a new and difficult problem — new and difficult, that is, in the sense that ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dash where 'namely' is implied
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a 'namely' is implied before a parenthetical or complementary clause, a dash should preferably be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope —...' Prefer dash to introduce such enumerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final summarizing clause preceded by dash
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken up into clauses, the final — summarizing — clause should be preceded by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given with a series of poets culminating in a summarizing clause preceded by a dash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash after side-heads and run-in heads
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should be used in connection with side-heads, whether 'run in' or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show side-head followed by dash introducing the paragraph text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash in place of 'to' for ranges; en/em dash distinctions and numeric contraction rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash in place of the word 'to' connecting two words or numbers (use en dash for month ranges, em dash for other cases). In connecting consecutive numbers, omit hundreds from the second number unless the first ends in two ciphers; special rule for B.C. dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: May–July, 1906 (en dash); May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906 (em dash); pp. 3-7 (en dash). Numeric contraction examples: 1880-95, pp. 113-16; 387-324 B.C. with note about repeating hundreds for B.C. dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash precedes reference after direct quotation in footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a dash precede the reference (author, title of work, or both) following a direct quotation, consisting of at least one complete sentence, in footnotes or cited independently in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I felt an emotion ...' — Thirty Years, 1, 379.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not combine dash with other internal punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash should not ordinarily be used in connection with any other point, except a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: 'DEAR SIR:— I have ...' or mixing comma and dash around the same insertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses for enumerative markers and structured lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Place between parentheses figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If divisions are paragraphed, a single parenthesis is ordinarily used with a lower-case (italic) letter; a period with figures and capital letters. A recommended scheme of notation and indention for syllabi and similar matter is provided (A., I., 1., a), (1), (a), etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses not ordinarily for parenthetical clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion might arise from the use of less distinctive marks, or unless the content of the clause is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dashes or commas depending on the logical and structural relation; examples given when parentheses are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used (i) to inclose an explanation or note, (2) to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, (3) to rectify a mistake, (4) to supply an omission, and (5) for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples for each use are provided, including editorial insertions and corrections within quoted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use brackets for 'continued' markers and typographical styling
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'To be continued,' at the end, and 'Continued from ...' at the beginning of articles, chapters, etc., should be placed between brackets, centered, and set in italics and in reduced type size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 320] [To be concluded]. See rules on reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses indicate omission or lacunae
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses are used to indicate the omission, from a quotation, of one or more words not essential to the idea to be conveyed, and to indicate illegible words, mutilations, and other lacunae in quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence four periods, separated by a space (en quad), should ordinarily be used (except French uses three). If the preceding line ends in a point, do not include it in the four. For omitted whole paragraphs or lines in poetry, insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads; periods should not extend beyond the length of the longest type-line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis treated as part of citation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as a part of the citation; consequently should be enclosed in the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow with examples and relation to quoted material.
